result: DMD-4 is one of ten DMRT proteins in C. elegans, with DMD-4 and DMD-5 being phylogenetically conserved in vertebrates. Neither the expression nor function of DMD-4 had been previously described.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the phylogenetic context and novelty of the study. C1 and C2 are supported by citations to prior phylogenetic analyses (Volff et al., 2003; Wexler et al., 2014), and C3 establishes the novelty of the current work. These claims provide appropriate background context.

result: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in a sexually dimorphic manner in adult phasmid neurons (PHA and PHB) of hermaphrodites but not males, and in a non-dimorphic manner in head sensory neurons and pharyngeal/alimentary tissues. The sexual dimorphism results from male-specific downregulation during the L4-to-adult transition.
evaluation: Claims C4-C15 describe the expression pattern of DMD-4::GFP based on microscopy of a CRISPR-tagged endogenous locus (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The developmental time-course data (C12-C14) supports the conclusion that dimorphism arises from male-specific downregulation (C15). The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: Null alleles of dmd-4 (ot933, tm1951) cause highly penetrant embryonic lethality and stuffed anterior intestine in escapers, while a deletion preserving the DNA-binding domain (ot896) shows no lethality.
evaluation: Claims C16-C20 describe phenotypes of different dmd-4 alleles. The embryonic lethality of ot933 is quantified in Figure 2A with statistical analysis. The stuffed intestine phenotype (C18) and hmc defects (C19) are documented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The viability of ot896 (C20) demonstrates domain-specific requirements.

result: The third intron of dmd-4 contains the cis-regulatory element for nervous system expression. Deletion of this enhancer (ot957ot935 allele) eliminates neuronal expression while preserving pharyngeal expression and viability.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23 describe the generation of a nervous system-specific knockout. C21 is supported by transgenic reporter assays (Figure 2B), C22 by microscopy of the engineered allele (Figure 2C), and C23 by quantification showing no lethality or intestinal defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B). This elegant genetic approach enables tissue-specific functional analysis.

result: The dmd-4(ot957ot935) nervous system-specific mutant shows normal neuronal specification, morphology, neurotransmitter identity, and head sensory neuron behaviors.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish that dmd-4 is not required for general neuronal development. Multiple cell-type markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and chemotaxis assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) support these conclusions. This is important for interpreting subsequent synaptic connectivity defects as specific rather than secondary to developmental abnormalities.

result: Phasmid neurons display sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity. Juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity that is sculpted during sexual maturation through activity-independent synaptic pruning and maintenance.
evaluation: Claims C28-C33 establish the developmental context for synaptic dimorphism. C28 is supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 1C, Cook et al., 2019; Jarrell et al., 2012). C29-C30 are supported by prior GRASP/iBLINC studies (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016). C31-C33 demonstrate activity-independence using genetic silencing and unc-13 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

result: dmd-4 functions cell-autonomously in phasmid neurons to promote hermaphrodite-specific synaptic pruning. In dmd-4 mutants, male-specific synapses fail to be pruned in hermaphrodites, while hermaphrodite-specific connections are unaffected.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe the core synaptic phenotype. GRASP data (Figure 3A-C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) show selective defects in pruning male-specific PHB>AVG synapses (C35) while hermaphrodite-specific connections are normal (C34). RAB-3 puncta quantification (C36-C37) corroborates the GRASP results. Cell-autonomous rescue (C38) confirms presynaptic function. Statistical analyses support all quantitative claims.

result: dmd-4 mutant hermaphrodites display partial masculinization of adult SDS avoidance behavior, with no defects in juvenile stages.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 link synaptic defects to behavior. C40-C41 cite prior work establishing the behavioral assay. C42-C43 show stage-specific behavioral defects (Figure 4A) that parallel the timing of synaptic pruning defects. The behavioral phenotype is intermediate between wild-type hermaphrodites and males, consistent with incomplete masculinization. Statistical analysis supports the quantitative claims.

result: The terminal selector transcription factor CEH-14 is required for dmd-4 expression in phasmid neurons. Loss of ceh-14 phenocopies dmd-4 mutants in causing masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 establish spatial control of dmd-4 expression. C44 is supported by microscopy showing selective loss of DMD-4::GFP in phasmid neurons of ceh-14 mutants (Figure 5A). C45-C46 link this to behavior, with C46 citing prior work (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016). This places dmd-4 downstream of a known phasmid neuron specification factor.

result: Constitutive panneuronal expression of LIN-41 maintains DMD-4 in adult male phasmids, demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway regulates the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 establish temporal control via the heterochronic pathway. C47 is supported by microscopy of transgenic animals expressing LIN-41 (Figure 5B), showing ectopic DMD-4 maintenance in adult males. C48 is a reasonable inference from this gain-of-function experiment. The data directly demonstrate that LIN-41 is sufficient to prevent DMD-4 loss.

result: The sex determination transcription factor TRA-1 promotes DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons. Loss of tra-1 causes DMD-4 downregulation in hermaphrodites, while forced TRA-1 expression maintains DMD-4 in males.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 establish sexual control via TRA-1. C49 is supported by microscopy of tra-1(e1099) pseudomales (Figure 5C). C50 is supported by transgenic expression of activated TRA-1 (Figure 5D). C51-C52 are reasonable inferences from these loss- and gain-of-function experiments. The bidirectional genetic manipulations provide strong support.

result: DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not controlled transcriptionally but rather post-transcriptionally at the level of protein stability/degradation, as demonstrated by non-dimorphic transcriptional reporters and dimorphic cDNA expression.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 establish post-transcriptional regulation. C53 shows the transcriptional reporter is expressed in both sexes (Figure 6A). C55 shows that cDNA with heterologous UTR still exhibits dimorphic expression (Figure 6B). C54, C56-C57 are logical inferences from these observations. This is a key mechanistic insight that redirects investigation toward protein-level regulation.

result: The DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (ubiquitin-binding domains) and contains three alpha-helices, with helices 1 and 3 predicted to form a ubiquitin-binding surface.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 establish the structural basis for ubiquitin binding. C58 is supported by HHsearch analysis (Figure 7A). C59 cites prior work on CUE domain classification. C60-C61 are based on homology modeling (Figure 7B). While homology models have inherent uncertainty, the prediction is reasonable given the sequence similarity and is subsequently validated experimentally.

result: The DMA domains of C. elegans DMD-4 and human DMRT3 bind monoubiquitin with ~400 μM affinity, similar to CUE domains. The L31R mutation abolishes binding. The DMD-4 DMA domain behaves as a monomer.
evaluation: Claims C62-C68 provide biochemical validation of ubiquitin binding. SPR data (Figure 7C) demonstrate binding of both DMD-4 and DMRT3 DMA domains to ubiquitin (C62-C63, C65) with affinities comparable to CUE domains (C66). The L31R mutation disrupts binding (C64, C68), validating the predicted binding interface. SEC-MALS data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) show the DMD-4 DMA domain is monomeric (C67). The biochemical data are rigorous and well-controlled.

result: Mutation of the ubiquitin-binding site (L31R, ot990 allele) causes loss of DMD-4 expression in neurons of both sexes at all stages, suggesting that ubiquitin binding is required for DMD-4 stability and that male-specific degradation may result from loss of ubiquitin-mediated stabilization.
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 demonstrate the functional importance of ubiquitin binding in vivo. Microscopy of the ot990 allele (Figure 7D) shows complete loss of neuronal DMD-4 in both sexes (C69-C70). GRASP data show synaptic pruning defects (C71, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). C72 is a well-supported inference from these data. C73 is more speculative but reasonable. The unexpected result that disrupting ubiquitin binding causes protein loss (rather than preventing degradation) is a key finding.

result: The ubiquitin-binding mutation affects DMD-4 stability differently in different tissues and at different times: constitutively required in neurons, but only required in adulthood in pharyngeal/alimentary tissues. Multiple DMA domain mutations show similar phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C74-C80 reveal tissue- and stage-specific requirements for ubiquitin binding. Microscopy of ot990 (Figure 7D) shows differential effects in neurons vs. pharynx (C74-C75). The lack of lethality or intestinal defects (C76-C77, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) indicates sufficient pharyngeal function during development. Additional DMA mutations (ot966, ot967, ot968) show similar phenotypes (C78, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). C79-C80 are reasonable inferences summarizing these complex spatiotemporal requirements.

result: The human DMRT3 DMA domain binds ubiquitin with similar affinity to DMD-4, but unlike DMD-4, the DMRT3 DMA domain can homodimerize.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 extend the biochemical analysis to human DMRT3. SPR data (Figure 7C) demonstrate ubiquitin binding (C81). SEC-MALS data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) show dimerization (C82). These data suggest conserved ubiquitin-binding function but divergent oligomerization properties between C. elegans and human proteins.

result: Human DMRT3::GFP expressed in C. elegans is not degraded in head neurons but is constitutively degraded in phasmid neurons of both sexes at all stages, without sexual or temporal control.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 test whether human DMRT3 is subject to similar regulation in C. elegans. Microscopy of transgenic animals (Figure 7F) shows differential stability in head vs. phasmid neurons (C83-C84) but loss of sex-specific regulation (C85). This suggests partial conservation of regulatory mechanisms but incomplete recapitulation of endogenous DMD-4 regulation.

result: The phylogenetically conserved DMRT gene dmd-4 plays a critical role in sculpting sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity by functioning sex-specifically in phasmid neurons to promote hermaphrodite-specific synapse pruning.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 summarize the main findings. C86 is supported by phylogenetic analysis (C1-C2). C87-C89 are supported by the synaptic connectivity data (C34-C39) and expression data (C4-C15). This is a well-supported summary of the core biological findings.

result: DMD-4 differs from other DMRT proteins (DMD-5, DMD-11) in three ways: it promotes synapse maintenance rather than pruning, functions presynaptically rather than postsynaptically, and is hermaphrodite-specific rather than male-specific.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93 compare DMD-4 to other DMRT proteins. C90 is supported by the synaptic data (C35). C91-C92 cite prior work on DMD-5/DMD-11. C93 is supported by the rescue experiments (C38). These comparisons highlight the distinct function of DMD-4 among C. elegans DMRT proteins.

result: DMD-4 is expressed specifically in hermaphrodites, contrasting with the male-specific expression of all other dimorphically expressed C. elegans DMRT proteins (DMD-5, DMD-11, MAB-3, MAB-23, DMD-3).
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 emphasize the unique sexual specificity of DMD-4. C94 is supported by expression data (C4-C15). C95-C96 cite prior work. This establishes DMD-4 as the first hermaphrodite-specific DMRT protein identified in C. elegans, which is conceptually important.

result: dmd-4 is required for viability due to non-dimorphic functions in the feeding organ. This function is conserved in dmd-4 orthologs (DMRT93B in arthropods, Dmrt3 in vertebrates), with mouse Dmrt3 knockouts dying from feeding defects.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 establish conserved non-dimorphic functions. C97 is supported by the lethality and intestinal phenotypes (C16-C19). C98-C99 cite prior work on orthologs. This demonstrates that dmd-4 has both sexually dimorphic neuronal functions and conserved non-dimorphic developmental functions.

result: Sex-specific transcription factor degradation has been observed for TRA-1 in C. elegans and Lola in Drosophila, indicating this is not an unprecedented mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 provide context by citing prior examples of sex-specific protein degradation. Both claims cite appropriate prior work (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006; Sato et al., 2019). This contextualizes the DMD-4 findings within known regulatory mechanisms.

result: The DMA domain is an evolutionarily ancient domain that was characteristic of the three ancestral DMRT gene clusters, arose before eumetazoans, but has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 establish the evolutionary context of the DMA domain. C102 is based on phylogenetic analysis. C103-C105 cite prior phylogenetic work (Mawaribuchi et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 2014). This establishes the ancient origin and variable retention of the DMA domain across evolution.

result: In C. elegans, dmd-4 is the only gene encoding a DMA domain, which is required for protein stability and binds monoubiquitin. Human DMRT3 also undergoes posttranslational regulation in worms, suggesting conserved molecular function.
evaluation: Claims C106-C110 summarize the molecular findings. C106 is based on genome analysis. C107-C108 are supported by the mutant and biochemical data (C69-C72, C62-C68). C109 is supported by the DMRT3 expression data (C83-C85). C110 is a reasonable inference from the combined data on C. elegans and human proteins.

result: CUE domains have diverse regulatory functions through ubiquitin association. Some non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domains stabilize proteins, as exemplified by yeast Met4, where the ubiquitin-binding domain prevents degradation.
evaluation: Claims C111-C114 provide mechanistic context by citing prior work on CUE domains and ubiquitin-mediated protein stabilization. All claims cite appropriate literature (Bagola et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2006; Davies et al., 2003; Prag et al., 2003; Flick et al., 2006; Heessen et al., 2005; Heinen et al., 2011, 2010). The Met4 example is particularly relevant as a precedent for the proposed DMD-4 mechanism.

result: By analogy to Met4, ubiquitin binding to DMD-4 may prevent protein degradation.
evaluation: Claim C115 is explicitly presented as a hypothesis based on analogy to Met4. While the analogy is reasonable given the similar phenotypes (loss of ubiquitin binding causes protein degradation), the actual mechanism by which ubiquitin binding stabilizes DMD-4 is not demonstrated. The claim is appropriately tentative but requires further experimental validation.

result: Ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of DMD-4 is susceptible to three parameters: sexual identity, cell-type, and developmental time. In wild-type animals, DMD-4 is only degraded in male phasmid neurons at a specific developmental stage.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119 synthesize the spatiotemporal regulation of DMD-4. C116 is an inference from the combined data. C117-C119 are directly supported by the expression data (C4-C15, C69-C80). This synthesis effectively captures the complex regulation of DMD-4 stability.

result: The DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction may be dynamically controlled in phasmid neurons, with destabilization as the default state that is antagonized by LIN-41 in juveniles and TRA-1 in adult hermaphrodites. Forced expression of either factor prevents degradation in adult males.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 propose a model for dynamic regulation. C120-C121 are speculative but reasonable hypotheses based on the ot990 phenotype (C69-C73). C122 is a well-supported inference from the LIN-41 data (C47-C48). C123 is speculative but consistent with all data. C124 is directly supported by the transgenic experiments (C47, C50). While some aspects are speculative, the model is well-grounded in the experimental data.

result: Different tissues show different requirements for ubiquitin-mediated DMD-4 stabilization: head neurons always require it, while pharynx/hmc only require it in adulthood.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 describe tissue-specific differences in regulation. C125 is an inference from the constitutive loss of DMD-4 in head neurons of ot990 mutants (C70). C126 is speculative but reasonable. C127 is a well-supported inference from the stage-specific loss in pharynx/hmc (C74-C75). These claims effectively capture the complexity of tissue-specific regulation.

result: Different C. elegans DMRT proteins use similar regulatory pathways (terminal selectors, TRA-1, LIN-41) but in fundamentally different ways. For mab-3/dmd-3, regulation is transcriptional and post-transcriptional (mRNA level); for dmd-4, regulation is post-translational (protein stability).
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 compare regulatory mechanisms across DMRT proteins. C128 is supported by the ceh-14 data (C44) and cites prior work. C129-C130 cite prior work on mab-3/dmd-3 regulation. C131-C132 are supported by the expression and stability data (C53-C57, C69-C80). C133 is a reasonable inference. This comparison effectively highlights the mechanistic novelty of dmd-4 regulation.
